UMich has been collecting party data for four earlier midterms (2006, 2010, 2018 and 2022), and none came close in terms of the party swing. 

Republicans’ 11.6-point drop is the biggest election-month decline, topping 7.8 points in 2006, when Democrats took both chambers under President George W. Bush. In 2018, the last time Democrats flipped the House under President Trump, Republican expectations fell just 5.1 points while Democrats’ dipped 0.6. 

Independents’ 10.7-point gain compares with a previous best of 0.5 point in 2010. 

For the overall index, the 4.1-point gain in expectations is the biggest in a midterm November since 2002, and the 3.5-point gain in sentiment the biggest since 2010.

Per the party tables released with the UMich survey, independents’ expectations jumped 10.7 points to 52.8, the highest since December 2025, and Democrats’ rose 7.1 to 42.4, the highest since January 2025. Meanwhile Republicans’ fell 11.6 points to 76.6, the lowest since October 2024, before the last presidential election.

That cut the gap between Republican and Democratic expectations to 34.2 points from 52.9, the narrowest since November 2024. 

Independents’ overall sentiment rose to 51.4 from 42.4, the highest since September 2025. The national numbers have tracked independents closely according to a May special report.

@C_Barraud's Top Macro Charts of the Week included a ZeroHedge write-up of the weekly rundown from Goldman's trading desk that I have been posting some charts from this weekend (you can click through for the article). They note Goldman's Panic Index ended the week at a record 9.8 after the fifth-biggest weekly VIX spike on record.

The VIX jumped 16.59 points last week to 35.89, behind only the weeks ending Oct. 10, 2008, Apr. 4, 2025, Feb. 28, 2020 and May 7, 2010.

What the S&P 500 did after those four (Goldman data):
▪️ Next day: higher in 3 of 4, averaging +5.1%.
▪️ Two weeks: higher just once, median −2.3%.
▪️ One month: higher in 2 of 4, median −1.1%.
▪️ Six months: higher in 3 of 4, median +13.9%.
▪️ One year: higher all 4 times, median +26.4% (vs. +11.9% for all days).

It's only four cases, and 2008 kept falling for months. But it's basically the same pattern as most of the panic signals I have been posting about the past few days: a choppy next few weeks, then a much better six-to-12-month setup.

That also dovetails with the desk's bottom line: "Technical indicators point to a potential near-term bounce, but further out the market is going to continue to face challenges until we get further clarity on the Feds path and the future of the AI trade."

Micron ($MU) closed at $594.73 Friday, down 13.9% on the day and 51% below its June record. A common refrain is that the low P/E makes sense: the earnings are "fake" peak-cycle profits, and "this is how semis always trade at the top." So I wanted to put some numbers on what the current price actually implies.

There's little question a lot of downside is priced in:

▪️ MU trades at 3.4x FY27 consensus EPS of $176.50 and 2.9x FY28's $207.76. Strip out $68B of net cash (~$59/share) and it's 3.0x FY27.
▪️ Cut those estimates in half, forever, and MU is still at just 6.7x FY27 (6.1x ex-cash), a 16.5% earnings yield on the haircut numbers.
▪️ Value that haircut EPS ($88.25) as a flat, no-growth stream at a 10% cost of equity and you get ~$942/share (+58% from current prices). At 12% it's ~$795.
▪️ Even assuming only 75% of earnings become free cash flow (FY26 was 72%), it's $721 at 10% and $611 at 12%.
▪️ Run it in reverse: at a 10% cost of equity, the price implies perpetual EPS of ~$54. That's 70% below FY27 consensus, 74% below FY28 and ~29% below the $75.52 Micron actually earned in FY26. At 12% it's ~$64, a 64% cut.

So the real question if you're a bear is, if this is the top, what kind of top this is. Micron's own history (GAAP EPS) offers two templates:
▪️ 2000: Micron earned $2.56 in FY2000, lost money for three straight years and didn't top that EPS until FY2017, 17 years later. Over the 16 years in between it averaged a small loss. Replay that (roughly zero EPS for 16 years, then back to the FY28 consensus) and the stock is worth ~$447 at 10% and ~$284 at 12%, 25% to 52% below here, and that assumes a full recovery at the end.
▪️ 2018: Micron earned $11.51 at the FY18 peak. The next three years averaged $4.34/yr (38% of peak) and the next seven averaged $3.39/yr (29%). It didn't get back above the FY18 level until FY26, and only because of the AI boom. Assume no rescue this time, with EPS stuck at 29% of the FY28 consensus (~$60) forever, and the stock is worth $662 at 10% and $562 at 12%.

That 2018 range brackets Friday's close. So arguably the bear case isn't being ignored, it's fully priced: at ~$595 the market is pricing a 2018-style bust with no recovery, ever. For the stock to be expensive here, this has to be 2000, not 2018. Anything milder than 2018 is upside: even the permanent 50% haircut above is worth $795 to $942.

Which gives the bulls a lot of reason to be bullish. Micron has a good case for "it's different this time." The company says long-term Strategic Customer Agreements will be over 35% of revenue through 2030, customer financial commitments total $32B (mostly cash prepayments), and over 75% of FY27 output is already committed.

There are also caveats to the reported numbers: FY27 capex is guided above $45B, so free cash flow will lag earnings during the buildout, and $12.7B of the cash is customer deposits. At 75% conversion, the 2018 scenario drops to $436 to $511, slightly below today's price. But the 50% haircut is still $611 to $721, at or above it.

Next test: FQ1 results, expected December 16 (guide: $61.5B revenue, $38.15 EPS).

BTIG's Jonathan Krinsky said Friday morning the selloff was "80% full" and a short-term bottom should come in the next few days around S&P 7,000.  The index didn't wait around. It fell 3.7% to 6,910 for a seventh straight loss, the longest losing streak since February 2020.

While Krinsky's persistent bearishness has given him a spotty record the past couple of years, he's often gotten the first move right. Now his bigger point is that even after a tactical low and a relief rally, the final low is probably still ahead:

▪️ History: He found only three six-day losing streaks in 30 years that closed just below the 200-day: September 2000, October 2018 and February 2020. All three were higher five days later. All three then saw "meaningful downside."
▪️ Breadth: About half of S&P stocks were still above their 50-day moving averages Thursday. At 20 lows after pullbacks of 8% or more since 1997, the median share above the 50-day was 11%. The highest was 44% (August 2024) and the next highest 25%. He calls a final low with half the index above the 50-day "unprecedented."
▪️ Apple: The biggest stock was 3.2% off its 52-week high Thursday and only about 5% off after Friday. At 10 S&P bottoms since 2015, Apple was a median 23% off its high and never closer than 11.8%.
▪️ The bounce he expects: 4% to 5% from about 7,000, back toward the 200-day near 7,348. He'd "use that strength to fade."

I ran his three precedents forward. The bounces topped out at 2% to 5%. From the sixth day's close, the S&P then fell another 11% to 25% at its low within about four months. So far we're still waiting for the bounce.

Sentiment is stretched enough for a bounce: the Daily Sentiment Index hit its lowest since April 2025 Thursday, and the VIX curve was the most inverted since spring 2025. But until breadth washes out and Apple catches down, a rally toward 7,350 is one Krinsky says to sell, not chase.
